narrative:
The model predicts you have a 16% chance of failing your final year, which is low enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution to help you succeed.

The prediction that you will fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, having zero failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees the absence of any prior setbacks as not providing the extra motivation or study habits that students with some past struggle often develop.

The second most important influence is your low amount of free time after school. This also pulls the prediction toward failing. While many passing students report medium or high free time, your lower level suggests you may be stretched thin, leaving less energy for focused academic work.

Third, the fact that you do want to pursue higher education works in your favor and pushes the model toward passing, but not strongly enough to overcome the other two factors.

To improve, consider using your limited free time more deliberately for structured study sessions, perhaps by creating a weekly schedule that protects consistent revision time. Since you have no history of failure and clearly aspire to continue studying, building steady routines now can turn your ambition into the results you need and potentially avoid the remedial requirement next time.
